summary: Mitsubishi's first new EV in Australia in more than a decade is a Taiwanese-built small SUV based on the Foxtron Bria, sold in three rear-drive grades and a 342kW dual-motor GSR, all on one 57.7kWh LFP battery. Early Australian previews praise its roomy rear seat, physical climate buttons and sharp launch pricing against the Kia EV3 and BYD Atto 3, but call the 320-litre boot compromised and the interior plastics and vinyl trim cheap-feeling; full local road tests had not been published at launch.
pros: Priced from $46,740 before on-road costs for the LS ($45,990 drive-away under the national launch offer), undercutting the Kia EV3 Air Standard Range at $47,600 with 403km of WLTP range against the Kia's 436km
The GSR's twin motors make 342kW and 700Nm for a claimed 3.9-second 0-100km/h, making it the quickest Mitsubishi sold in Australia at $64,990 before on-roads
A 2800mm wheelbase on a 4315mm body gives what Chasing Cars calls generous rear legroom, and physical buttons for climate and recirculation sit under the touchscreen

Mitsubishi advertises a 10-year/200,000km warranty and 10 years of capped-price servicing, but only if every service is done at a Mitsubishi dealer; otherwise cover is 5 years/100,000km. The battery is separately warranted for 8 years/160,000km to 70% capacity
cons: The 320-litre boot is small for the class (the Renault Scenic E-Tech carries 545 litres), and the 30-52 litre frunk is only fitted to the Aspire and above
A single 57.7kWh LFP pack across the range means the GSR's range falls to 328km WLTP, and DC charging peaks at 134kW with AC limited to 6.6kW
Preview reviewers found hard, untextured interior plastics, vinyl upholstery on the $53,990 Aspire and no sunblind for the panoramic roof
No braked towing capacity had been published at launch, so it cannot be relied on to pull a trailer
An unproven nameplate built by Foxtron, Foxconn's car arm, with no local resale history; the launch drive-away offer runs to an undisclosed end date
